title: The Royal Albert Hall’s echo took 98 years and a ceiling of giant ‘mushrooms’ to fix

cover.alt: Dozens of large round fibreglass discs hanging below the domed ceiling of the Royal Albert Hall, lit pink and purple above the tiers of boxes.

body: Queen Victoria opened London’s Royal Albert Hall on 29 March 1871, and its acoustic problems became obvious at the very first concert: the huge oval hall under its glass dome threw back a strong echo. A canvas awning hung below the dome didn’t cure it, and nor did fluted aluminium panels in 1949. The fix finally came in **1969**, when large fibreglass acoustic diffusing discs, nicknamed ‘mushrooms’ or ‘flying saucers’, were hung below the ceiling to scatter the sound instead of letting it bounce straight back.

slides.heading: Put the echo fixes in order, first to last
items: A canvas awning below the dome
slides.explanation: The awning came first and also kept the sun off the audience. The aluminium panels replaced it in 1949, and the discs went up in 1969.

slides.text: The only place where a British composer could be sure of hearing his work twice.
slides.attribution: Old joke about the Royal Albert Hall’s echo

slides.alt: The inside of the Royal Albert Hall seen from a box: red tiers of seats curving round the arena, the great organ behind the stage, and rows of pale discs hanging from the ceiling.
slides.caption: The hall from the Grand Tier. It seats 5,272, and behind the stage stands the organ known as the ‘Voice of Jupiter’.

slides.question: In what year were the ‘mushrooms’ finally hung?
slides.explanation: 1969, 98 years after the hall opened. Until then the acoustics were never properly tackled.

slides.label: pipes in the hall’s organ, the ‘Voice of Jupiter’, spread over 147 stops
slides.text: The Proms have been held in the hall every summer since 1941, after their old home, the Queen’s Hall, was destroyed in an air raid.
